summary.text: At the extra domain point \(n=0\), the divisor sums and totient are all zero, so the expression has value \(0\). But \(0\) is neither \(1\) nor prime, contradicting the claimed characterization of the zero values.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=\{d\in\mathbb N:1\le d<n+1\text{ and }d\mid n\}.
\]
For positive \(n\), this is the usual finite set of positive divisors of \(n\). Define
\[
\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\in D(n)}d,
\qquad
\sigma_2(n)=\sum_{d\in D(n)}d^2,
\]
and let \(\varphi(n)\) be the number of natural numbers \(r<n\) that are coprime to \(n\). The sequence expression is
\[
A(n)=\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma(n)-2n^2.
\]
In the formal statement under consideration, this expression is converted to a natural number after carrying out the subtraction over the integers. That conversion makes no difference in the counterexample below, because the integer expression will be exactly zero.

The statement that was formally conjectured quantifies over every natural number \(n\), not merely over the positive natural numbers. In particular, it asserts
\[
A(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\text{ or }n\text{ is prime}
\tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), together with a second equivalence characterizing when \(A(n)=2\). We disprove this universally quantified conjunction by taking
\[
n=0.
\]

First compute every term in \(A(0)\). By the definition of \(D(n)\),
\[
D(0)=\{d\in\mathbb N:1\le d<1\text{ and }d\mid0\}=\varnothing,
\]
because no natural number can satisfy \(1\le d<1\). Consequently both divisor sums are empty sums:
\[
\sigma(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d=0,
\qquad
\sigma_2(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d^2=0.
\]
Likewise, \(\varphi(0)\) counts natural numbers \(r<0\) that are coprime to \(0\). There are no natural numbers strictly below \(0\), so
\[
\varphi(0)=0.
\]
Finally, \(0^2=0\). Substitution therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(0)
&=\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma(0)-2\cdot0^2\\
&=0+0\cdot0-0\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the left-hand side of (1) is true at \(n=0\).

The right-hand side of (1), however, is false at \(n=0\). Indeed, its first alternative is \(0=1\), which is false. Its second alternative says that \(0\) is prime, which is also false: every prime natural number is at least \(2\), whereas \(0<2\). Hence
\[
0=1\text{ or }0\text{ is prime}
\]
is false.

Equivalently, if one assumes the universal conjecture and specializes (1) to \(n=0\), then the true equality \(A(0)=0\) forces the disjunction
\[
0=1\quad\text{or}\quad 0\text{ is prime}.
\]
There are two cases. In the first case one obtains the contradiction \(0=1\). In the second case one obtains the contradiction that \(0\) is prime. Thus both alternatives are impossible, and the assumed universal statement is false. There is no need to examine the separate assertion about the value \(2\): the conjectured statement is a conjunction for every \(n\), and its first conjunct already fails at \(n=0\).

Therefore the version quantified over all \(n\in\mathbb N\) is disproved by the explicit counterexample \(n=0\).

This scope qualification is essential. The canonical OEIS assertion is stated only for \(n\ge1\). Since \(0\) does not satisfy that hypothesis, the counterexample above does not disprove the correctly scoped positive-integer assertion. It disproves precisely the accepted formal version in which the restriction \(n\ge1\) was omitted.
